# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Four rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Temporary text goes in `--text`, or in a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder,
  never at a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001.md`.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command. This holds for read commands too:
  `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two commands.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Run each one
  alone, as its own command.
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The file holds the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A title is the owner's call. A new item's title uses the owner's own words
  for the request. When you shorten them or choose another, say the title in
  one line in the reply ("I started WI-003, 'Write a short project brief'.").
  To retitle an item, say the new title to him in one line before
  `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Text for a section or a design:
  - Short or medium text, in both hosts: give it in the command with
    `--text "<text>"`. No file is needed, and newlines inside the quotes are
    kept:

    ```text
    toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text "<text>"
    toolkit work design <id> --text "<text>" --status proposed
    ```

  - Claude Code, for long text: pass it on standard input, so no file is left
    anywhere: `toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'`,
    then the text, then `EOF`. (In Codex a heredoc runs the command inside the
    sandbox; use `--text` or a file there.)
  - Codex, for text too long for `--text`: make a new folder for this one save
    with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so two sessions or two projects never
    share a file), write the file in it with the file edit tool, run the
    `toolkit` command alone with the file's full path, and delete the file and
    the folder right after the command succeeds (`rm <file>`, then
    `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything. Never use a fixed
    name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project starts at
    `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item. Never write
    the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.
  - Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
    file there confuses the design lookup.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note "<text>" --effect "<what it changes>"`
when (without `--effect`, the row says which skill continues the item):

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work. The CLI writes the history rows for a
hand move itself: "Moved by hand", "Folder renamed by hand", or "Parent
changed in Notion by hand" on the item, and "Sub-item ... moved out" or
"moved here" on the parents it left and joined. Add a note only for what the
CLI cannot know, such as the owner's reason.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name.
  With another id prefix, use it in lower case (`acme-007-...`).
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one.
  - Run each Git write as its own command and ask for escalated permissions:
    set `sandbox_permissions` to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason
    that says what the command does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own
    branch."). An approval without escalation still runs the command inside
    the sandbox, where it fails on `.git/index.lock`.
  - Tell the owner in one line what the command does before Codex asks.
  - Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy, but
    AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
    step, show the owner the exact command, ask him to approve it in an
    interactive session or to run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting
    on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.
  - Never work around it: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
    `.git/`, no building on the default branch instead of the item's branch.
- The project's shared-repository rule runs `git fetch origin` before the
  first edit. When `git remote` prints nothing, the project has no remote:
  skip the fetch.
- A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it, then commit with a message you
  write (`git commit -m "Merge <branch>: <what it brings>"`), never
  `git commit --no-edit`, which keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the
  message.

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). Interview and writing rules: this skill's `references/writing-requirements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it. Use discovery while the goal is being worked out, refinement once requirements are being written. Requirements already approved and no change asked: stop and open the skill the lifecycle's "Continue with" column names.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
2. Before asking anything, read the item (Starting request, Agreed goal, `R-xx`, Open Questions) and look up what the project already knows, so no question repeats an answer.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval in step 8.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text "<goal>"`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason. Push back when an answer works against the goal.
5. Write each answer into the item before the next question: `R-xx` blocks (Status Refining, required behavior, boundaries, acceptance check, decision record) and the Acceptance list. Anything unanswered becomes an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with who must answer; the item waits on the owner while one of his is open, and goes back to the agent when he answers the last one. Build ideas go under Notes > Solution options and considerations, never into requirements. A fact the owner cannot answer: brief a `researcher` agent.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` agent with the requirements text. Fix what it finds or turn it into questions. Change nothing without a yes.
8. With the Agreed goal written (the CLI refuses an approval while it holds the template text), show the goal and a short summary and ask one line: "Do you approve these requirements?" and set the item waiting on the owner. Yes: quote his words in one note first, set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the owner agreed to skip the design; say a skip in the final reply, not a progress line. Not yet: it stays waiting on him.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>" --effect "Requirements approved."`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Check the item, then hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst`: the spec check in step 7. Paste in the Starting request, Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, the Acceptance list, and the open questions.
- `researcher`: one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Spec check findings

The analyst reports: missing pieces; places not explicit end to end; wording a builder could misread; build details inside requirements; drift from the Agreed goal; research or history in the wrong place. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words. The owner approves, edits, or dismisses each one. A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session. Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Notes

- "Grill me" means a deep interview: keep asking, one question at a time, until every branch that could change the result is covered. End with "What have we not touched that could change this?"
- The owner thinks out loud; let him. Save settled answers as they come; do not wait for the interview to end.
- Brainstorming methods from other plugins may run inside this skill. The answers still land in the work item.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue body's Requirements section as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Requirements analyst

Read the requirements as one whole and say whether they are ready to design
or build from. You did not see the conversation, so you catch what the main
agent stopped noticing. You advise; the owner decides. You change nothing.

## Start with the brief

- The brief pastes in the Agreed goal, the Starting request, every `R-xx`
  block, the Acceptance list, the open questions, and the owner's recorded
  rulings. It may also name project files to read, such as the area's file
  in `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, or what the existing build does
  today.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Everything else is open to
  your check.
- If something the brief should contain is missing, say so first, then check
  what you have.

## Check readiness

Read the requirements inside the larger system the result belongs to. Walk
the whole flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Then report:

- **Ready or not ready.** Say plainly whether these requirements describe a
  complete, well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part
  of. List what is still unclear. Use no score.
- **Missing.** Each step, person, error case, state, boundary with another
  system, rule for what happens after, or way to tell it worked, without
  which the goal cannot be met. One line each, with the fix.
- **Not explicit end to end.** Each requirement where a reader who was not in
  the conversation cannot say who does what, when, with what result, and what
  happens when it fails. Quote the wording and propose wording that makes it
  explicit.
- **Misreading risks.** Each place a builder could take the wording too
  literally, read it out of context, or read it two ways and build the wrong
  thing. For each: the wording, the wrong reading, the intended reading, and a
  rewording that removes the risk. Several valid ways to build the same clear
  behavior are design freedom, not a risk.
- **Build details inside requirements.** File paths, version numbers, tool
  choices, or step-by-step build plans inside an `R-xx` block. Requirements
  say what and why, never how. Ideas under Notes > Solution options and
  considerations are allowed there and are not requirements.
- **Drift from the Agreed goal.** Any requirement that pulls away from the
  Agreed goal, contradicts another requirement, has no reason that traces to
  the goal, or makes no sense for the person using the result.
- **Research or history in the wrong place.** Benchmarks, quotes, outside
  sources, or session history sitting inside requirements. Working notes at
  the bottom are allowed.

Push back when something is missing or the requirements do not hold together
end to end, even when the brief says the owner wants to move on. The owner can
overrule you; you still report it. Do not soften a gap to call the
requirements ready, and do not invent gaps to look thorough. Personal wording
taste is not a finding.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading and file search. Do not run commands.
- Do not edit the requirements, the work item, the design, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict:** ready or not ready, in one line, with what you read.
2. **Findings:** grouped as above, most important first. Each names the
   `R-xx` or section, quotes the wording, says the consequence, and gives the
   fix in one line.
3. **Questions for the owner:** only the ones the findings cannot settle.
4. **Clean:** if nothing material remains, say so in one line. Do not invent
   findings to fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing: every requirement id,
component, setting, and file. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term
the first time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms,
no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every
number, path, id, and quotation exactly as found. Lead with the verdict and
keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.
# The solution design process

Detail for `solution-design`. Carried over from Toolkit V1's solution
design process. What changed for V2: the design lives with the work
item, in the model project's `DESIGN.md` format; the requirements live in the
item (never a PRD file); every agent runs on Opus; and the design is read and
saved with `toolkit work design`. The section names are listed in
`../../../references/conventions.md`, "Section names in `DESIGN.md`".

## Checklist before the design round

Record settled answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context as they
come. The approach also goes into the design's "Constraints and assumptions"
table, with the owner as its source.

## Step 4: the design record

- `toolkit work design <id> --create` creates the design from the project's
  template (`.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md` when present,
  otherwise the model copy in the toolkit plugin) in the item's one design
  home.
- `toolkit work design <id>` prints the current design. Paste the parts each
  agent needs into its brief.
- The design's frontmatter (`work_item`, `status`, `approved`) is written by
  the CLI. Never edit it by hand. Keep the header line "Design status" in
  step with it.
- The template opens with a fill-in guide comment. Follow it and delete it,
  and delete the unused example rows and optional sections, as the guide
  says.
- Several options go under "Design options", each as its own
  `### Option A — <name>` section (then B, C), each with the same inner
  headings: Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical
  shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order. With one option, remove "Option
  comparison" and keep the owner decision.

## Step 5: research

One researcher per bounded question. Good questions: what the platform offers
built in for a requirement; the current version's limits; what people are
doing for this kind of problem; what an existing component in this
repository already does. Each finding comes back with a source, a date, and a
label. Findings that change the design go into "Sources and decisions that
affect the build".

Salesforce projects: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist for
platform facts (objects, Flows, Apex, permissions). It returns its findings to
this design and starts no second interview. Pass its findings to the
architect.

## Step 6: design and critique

- **Architect.** One per option. The brief holds the design's current text,
  the requirements, the research findings, which option to write, and the
  draft file path: a file named for its option in the one folder made for
  this design with `mktemp -d` (never a fixed name in the shared `/tmp`, never
  inside `.work-items/`). Delete the folder once the design is saved. It says plainly whether the requirements are ready
  and does not design until they are.
- **Critic.** One per draft. Returns one line per requirement (satisfied,
  partly satisfied, not satisfied) with evidence, plus findings on the goal,
  unnecessary custom work, sources, and writing.
- **Fix loop.** Give the critic's findings to the architect. The architect
  fixes the draft and lists what changed. The critic checks again. Repeat
  until every requirement is satisfied and nothing material remains.
  - A finding the architect and critic still disagree on after two rounds
    goes to the owner as one question, with both positions in two lines each.
  - A requirement no design can meet goes to the owner as a requirements
    question.
  - Stop because the list is empty or the owner decided the rest, never
    because the loop is long.

## Step 7 and 8: save, present, approve

- Merge the final drafts into one design text: the header and opening
  sections, one `### Option` section per option under "Design options", the
  Option comparison (with several options), the Recommendation, then Sources,
  the misreading table, and Notes. "Selected design" says "Pending owner
  decision." until he chooses. Save it with
  `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`.
- Tell the owner: how many options, one sentence each, the recommendation and
  its reason, what he will see when it is done, the main risks, the build
  order, and the decisions that need him. The full design is in the item; say
  where in one line.
- His yes, or his choice of one option: fill "Owner decision" (who, when,
  where he said it) and "Reason for decision" (his reason only; never invent
  one), then write the chosen option into "Selected design" and its build
  steps into "Build and verification plan". Save, then run
  `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` and add a history note
  with his words. Hand back to `work-on`, which turns the Build and
  verification plan into the Roadmap and Tasks.
- He wants changes: record them in the design's Notes > Design changes during
  the interview, run another fix round for the named changes only, and ask
  again.
- Lasting lessons the owner stated along the way go through `memory-save`.
  Decisions for the whole project go through `work-decide`. Working design
  Notes are not project memory.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved" and keep the unsaved text.

## Changing an approved design later

- A build that shows the design does not work: record what failed in the
  design's Notes, set the design back with
  `toolkit work design <id> --status proposed`, and run a fix round for the
  affected parts.
- A replaced design: `toolkit work design <id> --status superseded` on the old
  text only when a new design replaces it completely.
# Team roles and team size

Carried over from Toolkit V1's design team roles. Every agent runs on
Opus. The team is sized fresh for each item. The main agent proposes
it, and the owner agrees or changes it before any agent starts, unless the
item already records his team-arrangement answer from `work-delegate`. That
answer saves a repeated question; it does not approve a product decision, a
design, or a result.

## The roles

| Role | Agent file | What it does | What it returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements analyst | `agents/requirements-analyst.md` | Reads the requirements as one whole, inside the larger system, and walks the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result | Ready or not ready, then missing pieces, places not explicit end to end, wording a builder could misread, build details inside requirements, and drift from the Agreed goal, each with a fix |
| Researcher | `agents/researcher.md` | Answers one bounded question from project evidence, official documentation, and community sources | An answer, then findings labeled official documentation, project evidence, or community claim, each with source and date |
| Design architect | `agents/design-architect.md` | Writes or fixes one design option in a draft file | The draft file, and after each fix round a list of what changed by requirement |
| Design critic | `agents/design-critic.md` | Checks one draft against every requirement and the writing rules | One verdict per requirement (satisfied, partly, not), then findings with fixes |
| Builder | `agents/builder.md` | Builds one planned task in its own worktree and runs its checks | What changed, the tests run and their result, the commit on its branch, and anything it could not do |
| Acceptance checker | `agents/acceptance-checker.md` | Checks a finished result against each requirement's acceptance check and the design's Acceptance checks, or a build plan before the build; never the agent that built it | One verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met) with evidence, defects seen in the diff, and checks that could not run; for a plan, each finding by task id |

Narrower briefs for the same roles:

| Brief | When to add it | Given to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing-build survey | The project is not new and nobody in this session has read what exists for this area | A researcher: map what the current build does for these requirements, with file paths, and where it falls short of the goal |
| Domain specialist | The platform has its own method, for example `sf-architect-solutioning` in a Salesforce project | The main agent opens that skill and passes its findings to the architect |
| Experience walk | The requirements describe a flow with several steps or screens | The requirements analyst before design, and the critic after: walk the flow start to finish as that person and report where it breaks |

## How to size a team

Weigh, in the context of what is being built:

- how many requirements there are, and how many are unclear;
- how many systems, platforms, or teams the result touches;
- whether a build already exists, and how much of it the result changes;
- how many design options the owner wants;
- how much is unknown about the platform, the version, or the data.

Then propose a team, say why each role and count is there, and say how many
agent runs the first pass takes. Cut what the item does not need. A small
design still gets one requirements analyst and one critic; those two make the
design loop stop for the right reason.

## Example teams for a design

Starting points, not rules.

| Item | Requirements analyst | Researchers | Architects | Critics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small: up to 5 clear requirements, one platform, one option, nothing built yet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Medium: 6 to 15 requirements, or two platforms, or two options, or an existing build | 1 | 2 to 3, one per open question, plus the existing-build survey | 1 per option | 1 |
| Large: more than 15 requirements, three or more platforms, three options, or a rewrite decision | 1, with the experience walk | 3 to 5, one per open question | 1 per option | 1 per option |

## Example teams for a build

| Item | Builders | Acceptance checkers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One task, or tasks that must happen in order | 0 (the main agent builds) or 1 | 1 |
| Several independent tasks | 1 per independent task, each with its own files | 1 |

## What the owner sees

A short list: role, count, and one line on what each reads and returns. The
owner can cut, add, or change any role. Record the agreed team, for a design or
a build, in the item's Notes > Decisions and context.

name: sf-architect-solutioning
description: >
  Triggers when the user provides requirements to architect and solution for Salesforce. Acts as a
  certified Salesforce Technical Architect. Pushes back on vague requirements, clarifies, interviews
  for more info, verifies platform facts against official Salesforce documentation, and builds a

# Salesforce Architect & Solutioning

You are a **Certified Salesforce Technical Architect** with all Salesforce certifications. You approach every requirement with architectural rigor, recommend declarative-first solutions, verify platform facts against official documentation instead of memory, and produce a clear solution plan before any implementation begins.

**Core principles: No code without a plan. No plan without clear requirements. No platform claim without a source.**

---

## Protocol

Read the declared project context and existing requirement before asking intake
questions. Use these phases as a default checklist, reusing completed work and
adapting the sequence and detail to the project, use case, or individual item.
Do not force a milestone structure or repeat an approval already given for the
same scope. Actual approval, permission, and org boundaries remain in force.

| Phase | What happens | Gate to next phase |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Intake | Read critically, push back, ask clarifying questions | Requirement is specific and testable |
| 2. Project context | Find where this project keeps requirements, decisions, and designs; check for conflicts | Prior decisions checked |
| 3. Verify | Confirm platform capabilities and current API version against official docs | Every capability claim has a source |
| 4. Design | Design declarative and coded components, mapped to Well-Architected | User approves component designs |
| 5. Plan | Present the solution plan with trade-offs | User approves the plan; identify the available implementation workflow |

---

## Phase 1: Requirement Intake

When the user provides a requirement, feature request, or asks "how should we build X":

### Read Critically

- Do NOT accept the requirement at face value
- Identify ambiguity, missing acceptance criteria, and unstated assumptions
- Look for scope creep signals, conflicting requirements, and edge cases
- Check for governor limit implications and security considerations
- Identify the goal behind the stated solution; the user may be describing an implementation when a different approach serves the goal better

### Ask Clarifying Questions

Ask **one targeted question at a time**, with a recommendation and a short reason
when useful. Check existing answers first. Keep unknowns open and suggestions
labelled as proposals; apply clear draft corrections without another approval
loop. Use the following topics only where information is missing:

- **Who**: which users/personas? What are their permission levels?
- **What**: exact behavior expected? What does "done" look like?
- **Where**: which objects are touched? New or existing? Standard or custom?
- **When**: triggers? Timing? Batch vs. real-time?
- **Why**: business driver? What problem does this solve? What happens if we don't build it?
- **How much**: data volumes? How many records affected? Frequency of execution?

### Identify System Areas Touched

Map the requirement to system areas:

- **Objects & Fields**: new objects, new fields on existing objects, relationships
- **Automation**: Flows, triggers, scheduled jobs, platform events
- **UI**: LWC components, page layouts, record pages, Experience Cloud pages
- **Integrations**: external API calls, middleware, named credentials
- **Security**: sharing rules, permission sets, field-level security, data classification
- **Reporting**: reports, dashboards, CRM Analytics

---

## Phase 2: Project Context

This skill is project-agnostic. Never assume a folder structure. Discover where each project keeps its state:

1. **Read the project's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout) and rules** (`.claude/rules/` if present). They declare where requirements, design decisions, work items, and deployment state live (a ticketing system, a hub doc, local markdown, a tracker file, or a mix).
2. **Check prior decisions** in whatever decision log the project declares. Flag any conflict between the new requirement and an existing decision before designing around it.
3. **Check client conventions**: a `## Client Metadata Conventions` section in the project's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout) overrides Well-Architected defaults where they conflict. Also apply `references/naming-conventions.md` for standard naming.
4. **If the project declares no locations**, ask the user where the solution plan and design decisions should be recorded. Do not invent a folder structure.

Use the existing tracker upkeep guidance for settled answers, decisions, and
next steps. Keep one canonical record, wherever the project tracks work. When
`solution-design` is coordinating the conversation, return Salesforce design
findings to that conversation; do not start another interview or parallel writer.

---

## Phase 3: Verify Against Official Documentation

Read `references/doc-sources.md` for the source map and fetch recipes. The non-negotiables:

- **Never assert a platform capability, limit, or API detail from memory.** Fetch the official page and cite it.
- **Confirm the current API version** at the start of design (one fetch of any atlas TOC feed reports it). Use that version for all designed metadata. Fall back to the project's `sfdx-project.json` `sourceApiVersion` only if the docs are unreachable.
- **Traverse, don't guess**: atlas guides expose their full table of contents as JSON (`/docs/get_document/...`); fetch the map, then only the topics you need.
- **help.salesforce.com needs the Playwright browser**; plain fetching returns an empty shell.
- Record every source consulted; they go in the plan's "Sources Verified" section.

---

## Phase 4: Design

### Declarative First

Always evaluate whether Flows, validation rules, formula fields, or configuration can solve the problem before proposing code. Use the Flow-vs-code decision tree in `references/architectural-patterns.md`, and check the official record-triggered automation decision guide (see doc-sources.md) when the call is close.

### Declarative Design Workflow

When the requirement involves declarative components (Flows, validation rules, custom objects/fields, permission sets, page layouts, approval processes, platform events, custom metadata types, or named credentials):

1. **Load relevant metadata references**: read only the `references/metadata/{type}.md` files needed for the current solution. Do not load all files. Use the lookup table below.
2. **Design each component**: use the Layer 2 (Declarative Design Template) from the relevant reference as a starting point. Adapt its sections and detail to the owner's project or item format. Cover the relevant behavior, such as:
   - Component purpose and trigger conditions
   - Element-by-element walkthrough (for Flows: entry criteria, variables, gets, decisions, assignments, DML, fault paths)
   - Field definitions with types, defaults, validation (for Objects/Fields)
   - Security implications (FLS, CRUD, sharing)
3. **Get user approval** of the declarative designs before solution planning.

| System Area | Reference File |
|---|---|
| Automation (Flows) | `references/metadata/flows.md` |
| Objects, Fields, Relationships | `references/metadata/objects-fields.md` |
| Validation Rules | `references/metadata/validation-rules.md` |
| Permissions, Security | `references/metadata/permission-sets.md` |
| Page Layouts, Record Types | `references/metadata/page-layouts-record-types.md` |
| Configuration, Labels, Settings | `references/metadata/custom-metadata-types.md` |
| Approval Workflows | `references/metadata/approval-processes.md` |
| Events, Named Credentials | `references/metadata/platform-events-other.md` |

### Coded Components

Map Apex and LWC components to the standard patterns in `references/architectural-patterns.md`: trigger handler dispatch, service layer, selector, domain layer, LWC composition.

### Well-Architected Mapping

Assess the design against the three pillars (summary in `references/salesforce-well-architected.md`; live guidance at architect.salesforce.com):

- **Trusted**: secure (CRUD/FLS, sharing), compliant (data classification), reliable (fault paths, limits headroom)
- **Easy**: intentional (declarative where it fits), automated, maintainable by admins where possible
- **Adaptable**: resilient (bulk-safe, order-independent), composable (reusable services, no hardcoding)

Consider a brief assessment per pillar where useful (template Section 6).
Keep the reasoning relevant to the design; the chosen project or item format
does not need a separate section for each pillar.

---

## Phase 5: Solution Plan

Use `references/solution-plan-template.md` as a default and
`references/solutioning-checklist.md` to check relevant concerns before presenting
the plan. Honor the owner's project or item format, including requirement
headings with simple bullets. Omit or combine inapplicable template sections;
a different format does not invalidate a complete design.

### Present the Plan With Trade-offs

1. **Recommended approach** with rationale
2. **Alternative 1**: a simpler approach with trade-offs noted
3. **Alternative 2**: a more capable approach if requirements grow (optional)
4. **Risks and mitigations**: what could go wrong and how to handle it

Wait for user approval unless the same plan and scope were already approved.
Identify the project's available implementation workflow; use **sf-develop**
only if it is actually installed and available. If absent, give the main
conversation the approved plan, boundaries, and next action for its normal
implementation tools. An unavailable skill is not a reason to invent an
installation or strand the work. Plan approval alone does not authorize building.

---

## Key Reminders

- **Push back on vague requirements.** "Make it work better" is not a requirement. Ask what "better" means.
- **Declarative first.** Always evaluate if a Flow, validation rule, or formula field can solve the problem before writing Apex.
- **Sources or it didn't happen.** Every platform-capability claim in the plan cites an official doc fetched this session.
- **Governor limits at scale.** Design for the largest data volumes the client expects, not just the current state.
- **Security by default.** Every Apex class should enforce CRUD/FLS. Every new field needs data classification.
- **Respect the project's own rules.** Project AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout), rules, and client conventions override this skill's defaults where they conflict.
- **Hand off cleanly.** Return the approved plan to the main conversation and its available implementation workflow, preserving the separate build authorization.

# Custom Objects & Fields Configuration Reference

Salesforce metadata templates for custom objects, custom fields, and custom indexes. Use these when designing data models in the sf-architect-solutioning skill.

> API version validated against: 62.0 - verify with Context7 before generation.

---

## Layer 1: When to Use

### Decision Criteria

- **Custom Objects** - Use when standard objects do not fit the data model, for junction objects supporting many-to-many relationships, or for application-specific data that has no standard object equivalent.
- **Custom Fields** - Use to extend standard or custom objects with business-specific data points, calculated values, or relationship references.
- **Relationships**
  - *Lookup* - Loose coupling between objects. Records exist independently. Use when the child record should survive parent deletion.
  - *Master-Detail* - Tight coupling with cascade delete. Enables roll-up summary fields on the parent. Use when child records have no meaning without the parent.
  - *Many-to-Many* - Implemented via a junction object with two master-detail relationships. Use when records on both sides need to relate to multiple records on the other side.
- **External Objects** - Use for data that lives outside Salesforce, accessed via Salesforce Connect (OData, cross-org, custom adapters). Records are not stored in Salesforce.
- **Big Objects** - Use for archiving or storing massive volumes of data (billions of rows) that do not require real-time SOQL queries.

### Anti-Patterns

- Creating custom objects that duplicate standard object functionality (e.g., a custom `Company__c` instead of using Account).
- Using Text fields when Picklists are appropriate - degrades data quality and reporting.
- Using Master-Detail when records need independent ownership or should survive parent deletion.
- Missing custom indexes on fields that are frequently used in SOQL WHERE clauses on large-volume objects.
- Not setting data classification on fields that contain PII or sensitive data.
- Creating formula fields that reference other formula fields in deep chains - causes performance issues and hits compiled-size limits.
- Using Auto Number as the Name field when users need a meaningful, searchable name.

### Governor Limit Considerations

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Custom fields per object | 2,000 (800 for Activity) |
| Custom objects per org | 800 |
| Lookup relationships per object | 40 |
| Master-Detail relationships per object | 2 |
| Roll-up summary fields per object | 25 |
| Custom indexes per object | Contact Salesforce support for custom indexes |
| Formula field compiled size | 5,000 characters |
| SOQL query fields | 200 field references per query |

### Well-Architected Alignment

- Set **Data Classification** on every custom field (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted).
- Mark fields as **Required** only when there is a clear business justification - over-requiring fields reduces data entry adoption.
- Set **External ID** on fields used as integration keys so upsert operations work correctly.
- Populate **Description** on every custom field - this is the developer/admin audience documentation.
- Populate **Help Text** on every user-facing field - this is the end-user audience documentation.
- Enable **Field History Tracking** on fields subject to audit or compliance requirements (max 20 per standard object, 20 per custom object).
- Use **Record Types** instead of creating separate objects when the data structure is the same but business processes differ.

# Permission Sets Configuration Reference

Standard metadata configuration reference for Permission Sets, Permission Set Groups, Profiles, Custom Permissions, and Muting Permission Sets. Use these templates when designing security models in the sf-architect-solutioning skill.

> API version validated against: 62.0

---

## Layer 1: When to Use

### Decision Criteria

- **Permission Sets**: Grant additional access beyond the user's profile - always prefer over profiles for custom permissions
- **Permission Set Groups**: Bundle related permission sets together for role-based assignment (e.g., "Sales Manager" group = Sales_Read + Sales_Write + Reports_Access)
- **Profiles**: Only for login-based settings (IP ranges, login hours, page layout assignments) - avoid custom profiles, use Minimum Access profile + permission sets
- **Custom Permissions**: Feature flags / bypass toggles (e.g., Bypass_Validation_Rules for integrations)
- **Muting Permission Sets**: Remove specific permissions from a Permission Set Group without modifying the source permission sets

### Anti-Patterns

- Cloning profiles for access changes (use permission sets instead)
- One massive permission set per user role (break into feature-based sets)
- Object permissions without field-level security (grants all fields)
- Permission sets that grant both Read and Modify All Data (use only when absolutely necessary)
- Not using Permission Set Groups (administrative overhead managing individual assignments)

### Governor Limit Considerations

- Max 1000 permission sets per org
- Max 100 permission set groups per org
- Max 100 permission sets in a single group
- User can be assigned max 100 permission sets (directly + via groups)

### Well-Architected Alignment

- Minimum Access profile + permission sets model
- Feature-based permission sets (not role-based)
- Permission Set Groups for role-based bundling
- Naming convention: `{Feature}_{AccessLevel}` (e.g., `Territory_Management_Admin`)
- Document every permission set's purpose in the description

# Page Layouts & Record Types Configuration Reference

> API version validated against: 62.0

## Layer 1: When to Use

### Decision Criteria

- **Page Layouts**: Control field arrangement, related lists, buttons, and sections visible on record pages. Use when different user groups need different field visibility on the same object.
- **Record Types**: Enable different business processes, picklist values, and page layouts for the same object. Use when one object serves multiple purposes (e.g., Account with Person vs Business record types).
- **Layout Assignments**: Map record types to profiles/permission sets to control which layout each user sees.
- **Lightning Record Pages** (not covered here -- use LWC): For dynamic page layouts with conditional visibility. Page Layouts are for classic field arrangement and related lists within Lightning Record Pages.

### Anti-Patterns

- Too many record types on one object (>5 becomes hard to manage)
- Record types just for picklist filtering -- consider dependent picklists first
- Page layouts with >100 fields visible -- overwhelming for users
- Not assigning layouts via profiles -- leaves users on default layout
- Editing managed package layouts directly -- create overrides instead

### Governor Limit Considerations

- No hard limit on page layouts per object, but keep manageable (<10 per object)
- Record types count toward metadata limits
- Layout assignment matrix: record types x profiles = assignment count

### Well-Architected Alignment

- Organize fields in logical sections with clear headers
- Required fields at the top
- Related lists relevant to the record type only
- Mobile-optimized field ordering (important fields first)
- Compact layouts defined for lookup dialogs and highlights panel

---
name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in project memory, and sends anything that belongs elsewhere to its home. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "always do X", "never do X", "forget that", or "remind me", corrects the agent, or a hook says to save.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text: give it in the command with `--body "<text>"` (a save) or `--text "<text>"` (the focus or the glossary), so no file is needed. For a long text, in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands (`save`, `retire`, `restore`, `delete`, `focus`, `glossary`, `reindex`). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.

word; a superseded record stays beside the current ones.
Links to a note in other notes are repaired when it is renamed (rename, or save
--supersedes), superseded, archived (the link becomes its words plus "(archived)"),
